```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(knitr)

annual <- read_csv("output/tables/annual_gompertz_fits.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
windows <- read_csv("output/tables/age_window_sensitivity.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
models <- read_csv("output/tables/model_comparison.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
state_fits <- read_csv("output/tables/state_gompertz_fits.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
cause_change <- read_csv("output/tables/cause_rate_decomposition_2005_2023.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
life_decomp <- read_csv("output/tables/life_expectancy_decomposition_2005_2023.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

primary <- annual |>
  filter(population == "Total", sex == "Both", year %in% c(2005, 2019, 2022, 2023))
primary_latest <- primary |> filter(year == 2023)
cause_summary <- life_decomp |>
  group_by(cause) |>
  summarise(years = sum(years_contributed), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(years)
```

[![Rebuild analysis](https://github.com/tannerjared/Gompertz/actions/workflows/rebuild.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/tannerjared/Gompertz/actions/workflows/rebuild.yml)

This project asks a more precise question than whether mortality “doubles every eight years”:

> At what ages, in which periods and populations, and for which underlying causes has the acceleration of U.S. mortality changed?

The repository downloads official U.S. life tables, reconstructs a tidy analysis dataset, fits competing mortality models, examines age-window sensitivity, compares demographic groups and states, and decomposes mortality change by underlying cause of death. Every table and figure below is generated by the pipeline.

## Main findings

### One 30–80 slope conceals substantial age variation

Across ages 30–80, the fitted Gompertz doubling time increased from `r sprintf("%.1f", primary$doubling_time[primary$year == 2005])` years in 2005 to `r sprintf("%.1f", primary_latest$doubling_time)` years in 2023. That summary is mathematically correct for the selected interval but is not uniform across adulthood.

```{r sensitivity-table}
windows |>
  filter(population == "Total", sex == "Both",
         year %in% c(2005, 2019, 2022, 2023),
         window %in% c("30–49", "50–69", "70–89", "30–80")) |>
  select(Year = year, `Age window` = window, `Doubling time` = doubling_time) |>
  mutate(`Doubling time` = sprintf("%.1f years", `Doubling time`)) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = Year, values_from = `Doubling time`) |>
  kable()
```

![Age-window sensitivity](output/figures/age_window_sensitivity.png)

The major departure from the earlier curve is concentrated in younger adulthood. Later-adult slopes are much more stable. This makes a moving-window or age-segmented description more informative than a single “law” fitted over 50 years of age.

![Local doubling-time heatmap](output/figures/rolling_doubling_heatmap.png)

### The annual series shows when the divergence emerged

The original repository compared three years. This rebuild uses every final national life table from 2005 through 2023, including revised intercensal tables for 2005–2009.

![Annual doubling time](output/figures/annual_doubling_time.png)

![Age-period change](output/figures/age_period_change.png)

The heatmap emphasizes why period and age must be considered together: a slower fitted slope can occur because mortality rose at the younger end of the fitting interval, not because mortality improved more slowly at every adult age.

### Gompertz is a useful summary, not a universal fit

The analysis compares Gompertz, Gompertz–Makeham, quadratic Gompertz, Kannisto, and a four-degree-of-freedom natural spline over ages 30–95. Models are evaluated with corrected AIC and five-fold held-out-age prediction error; the complete values are in [`model_comparison.csv`](output/tables/model_comparison.csv).

![Model comparison](output/figures/model_comparison.png)

A high R² for a straight line on log mortality is not, by itself, evidence that curvature or late-age deceleration is absent. The residual and predictive comparisons explicitly test that assumption.

### Sex and population patterns are heterogeneous

NCHS has published annual life tables for five race/Hispanic-origin populations, by sex, since 2019. These classifications and the associated adjustments are properties of the official life tables and should not be interpreted as biological categories.

![Subgroup estimates](output/figures/subgroup_doubling_2023.png)

### Geographic variation is substantial

The state analysis fits ages 40–80 in the 2019 and 2022 state life tables. Because small states have noisier curves, the displayed slopes use a transparent normal–normal empirical-Bayes shrinkage step. It is descriptive and is not a causal state ranking.

![State change](output/figures/state_change.png)

### Underlying causes explain the younger-adult change

The cause analysis reads the NCHS mortality public-use files directly for 2005, 2019, 2022, and 2023. Mutually exclusive underlying-cause categories are used to allocate the corresponding all-cause life-table mortality rate at each age. This tests proposed explanations rather than inferring them from the shape of the all-cause curve.

![Cause-specific rate change](output/figures/cause_rate_change.png)

The project also applies a Horiuchi stepwise-replacement decomposition to restricted remaining life expectancy from age 30 through age 100. Positive bars contributed to improvement from 2005 to 2023; negative bars offset it.

![Life-expectancy decomposition](output/figures/life_expectancy_decomposition.png)

The numerical decomposition is in [`life_expectancy_decomposition_2005_2023.csv`](output/tables/life_expectancy_decomposition_2005_2023.csv). It is a decomposition of period mortality rates, not proof that any cause produced another cause or any individual outcome.

## Statistical approach

The published life-table quantity `qx` is the probability of dying between ages *x* and *x + 1*. Gompertz describes a mortality rate or hazard. For adult single-year intervals, the pipeline uses the inverse of the NCHS life-table relationship:

\[
m_x = \frac{q_x}{1 - q_x/2}.
\]

The primary summary fits

\[
\log(m_x) = \log(m_{50}) + \beta(x - 50),
\qquad T_2 = \frac{\log 2}{\beta},
\]

where centering at age 50 makes the intercept interpretable. The primary window is 30–80 for continuity with the original project, but every conclusion is accompanied by prespecified age-window and rolling-window sensitivity analyses.

Important qualifications:

- The intervals around slopes and doubling times measure lack of fit across ages. They are not official NCHS sampling intervals.
- The `100 and over` row has `qx = 1` because it is open-ended. It is excluded from annual-rate models and threshold interpolation.
- Period life tables describe a synthetic cohort exposed to one period’s age-specific rates. They do not follow the same people as they age.
- Cause categories are based on the single underlying cause recorded on the death certificate. Multiple-cause analyses can answer different questions.
- State shrinkage and subgroup comparisons are descriptive; they do not adjust for compositional or contextual confounding.

## Reproduce everything

Requirements are R 4.3 or later, `curl`, `unzip`, and `awk`. The release was built with R 4.6.1, and all package versions are recorded in `renv.lock`; continuous integration also uses R 4.6.1.

```r
install.packages("renv")
renv::restore()
targets::tar_make()
testthat::test_dir("tests/testthat")
```

The regular build downloads about 5–10 MB of official spreadsheets and recreates every derived dataset, table, figure, the README, and [`analysis/report.html`](analysis/report.html).

The committed `data-raw/cause_counts.csv` is a non-identifying aggregate created from roughly 500 MB of official mortality public-use archives. To rebuild that file from the original archives:

```r
source("scripts/rebuild_causes.R")
targets::tar_make()
```

Set `NCHS_INSECURE_SSL=true` only if an institutional machine has an incomplete certificate chain for `ftp.cdc.gov`; the default keeps certificate verification enabled.

## Repository layout

```text
R/                         import, modeling, decomposition, and plotting functions
config/                    prespecified years, age windows, groups, and source URLs
data-raw/                  aggregate cause counts and source checksum manifests
data/derived/              pipeline-generated tidy analysis datasets
output/figures/            publication-ready figures
output/tables/             complete numerical results
analysis/report.Rmd        full methods and results report
tests/testthat/            data and statistical regression tests
_targets.R                 end-to-end dependency graph
renv.lock                  exact R dependency versions
.github/workflows/         clean rebuild and test workflow
```

See [`DATA_SOURCES.md`](DATA_SOURCES.md) for provenance, revision choices, access dates, and redistribution notes. Optional cohort and international analysis functions accept licensed Human Mortality Database `Mx_1x1` files placed in `data-raw/hmd/`; HMD source files are not redistributed by this repository.

## Data sources and citation

- National Center for Health Statistics, [U.S. Life Tables](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/products/life_tables.htm), 2005–2023.
- National Center for Health Statistics, [U.S. State Life Tables](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/products/life_tables.htm), 2019 and 2022.
- National Center for Health Statistics, [Mortality Multiple Cause public-use files](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data_access/vitalstatsonline.htm), selected years 2005–2023.
- Human Mortality Database, [methods protocol](https://www.mortality.org/File/GetDocument/Public/Docs/MethodsProtocolV6.pdf), for optional licensed cohort and international extensions.
